title: Microstructural feature-driven post-mortem analysis of plastic strain and stress triaxiality in ductile-fractured ferrite-martensite dual-phase steel: Integrating microstructural observations and mesoscale finite element simulations
abstract: This study proposes a novel microstructural feature-driven post-mortem stress and strain derivation method, focusing on high-strength ferrite-martensite dual-phase (DP) steels under uniaxial tensile deformation. The method correlates the aspect ratio and microvoid fraction of deformed martensite islands with the macroscopic tensile strain and historical average stress triaxiality by combining representative volume element (RVE)-finite element (FE) simulations of virtual DP microstructures with observational results. The RVE-FE simulations incorporate a ductile fracture criterion for martensite islands, derived from high-pressure (400 MPa) tensile tests of specimens machined from two types of DP steels. This approach accurately reproduces the microvoid volume fraction, which is crucial for inversely deriving the stress triaxiality, while accounting for martensite island compression by the deformed ferrite matrix. The results of RVE-FE simulations of the tensile-fractured DP steels validated the ability of the method to determine the sub-millimeter-scale plastic strain after the occurrence of fracture. Furthermore, the post-mortem stress triaxiality, derived through combined analyses of the microvoid fraction and RVE-FE simulations, agreed quantitatively with the FE-simulated macroscopic values. These results demonstrate the potential of this method for analyzing incidental fractures in press-forming processes and its possible general application to various deformation modes simulating actual press-forming processes.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strength steel sheets (HSSs) have been developed for application in automotive crash-resistant components, and various improvements are currently being investigated [ 1–3 ]. Decreasing CO 2  emissions through weight reduction is a critical challenge in the automotive industry [ 4–6 ], and HSSs have significantly contributed to addressing this issue [ 7 , 8 ]. Increasing the tensile strength of component steel sheets allows for the design of thinner crash-resistant parts that retain their crash-worthiness [ 9 ], thereby achieving substantial weight reduction.

However, press-forming HSSs, as compared to mild steel sheets, is more challenging. Although HSSs experience issues such as deteriorated press-forming accuracy due to spring back [ 10–12 ] and tool damage [ 13–15 ], material fracture due to insufficient ductility has been particularly problematic [ 16–18 ]. The early stages of HSS adoption were characterized by the frequent occurrence of material fractures during press-forming [ 19 , 20 ]. Component shape design [ 21 , 22 ], press-forming technique [ 23–25 ], and material development [ 26–29 ] advancements have largely overcome these challenges, enabling the production of vehicles wherein HSSs constitute >50 % of the frame steel. The ever-increasing demand for higher strength in steel requires further research to overcome challenges specific to ultra-HSSs, such as delayed fracture due to hydrogen embrittlement [ 30–32 ].

Although HSSs have been successfully applied in automotive applications, challenges that cannot be resolved through laboratory studies persist, impacting mass productivity. A prime example of such a practical issue is “incidental fracture.” This phenomenon refers to material failure occurring approximately once in several hundreds or thousands of press-forming operations. This probabilistic material failure is characterized by unexpected spontaneous material fracture during production under apparently stable mass production conditions. Standard laboratory material evaluation techniques cannot reliably predict the risk of incidental fracture owing to its unpredictable occurrence. Therefore, experts metallurgically investigate the microstructure near the fracture sites to determine the causes of the incidental fractures. The influences of inclusions [ 33–35 ], crystal orientation [ 36 , 37 ], and microstructural topology [ 38–40 ] are often investigated to identify variations from ideal microstructures. These variations can lead to reduced ductility and ultimately contribute to material failure. However, the definitive causes are mostly inconclusive because an incidental fracture cannot be attributed to material factors alone. Unexpected irregularities in the strain or stress state imposed during press-forming, arising from unknown causes, can cause such fractures. Unlike material variations, identifying these mechanical irregularities from post-event material conditions is challenging. Moreover, the microstructure in the press-formed area becomes so complex that even distinguishing individual crystal grains is difficult [ 41–43 ], making it impossible to determine the stress and strain history of the structure through simple observations.

Accordingly, this study proposes a method to determine the plastic strain and historical average stress triaxiality in sub-millimeter scale observation fields. By clarifying whether unexpected excessive stress and strain were applied, causing the incidental fracture, through the proposed method, we can determine whether some malfunction occurred during press-forming or whether material variability may have lowered the fracture threshold itself. The method is based on morphological changes in martensite islands, including their fracture behavior, in ferrite-martensite dual-phase (DP) steel. This method leverages the fact that martensite, being a hard phase, remains microstructurally identifiable even after large deformation [ 42 , 44 , 45 ]. Szewczyk and Gurland [ 46 ] used the aspect ratios of martensite islands to evaluate their elongation during tensile deformation. Our proposed approach inverts this concept by using the observed aspect ratios to estimate the local tensile plastic strain in areas containing martensite.

Our method is characterized by the combination of finite element (FE) uniaxial tensile simulations of representative volume elements (RVEs) of a ferrite-martensite DP microstructure, with the observed martensite elongation. Establishing a relationship equation solely from observations is challenging owing to the variable correspondence between martensite elongation (measured as the change in the aspect ratio from the undeformed state) and the average strain in the observation field. Integrating RVE-FE simulations yielded a smooth function relating these two parameters. Hardness measurements can be used to estimate the local plastic strain near fracture surfaces; however, this approach has limitations. Work hardening in the strain regime where ductile fracture occurs is minimal [ 17 , 47 , 48 ] and, therefore, difficult to detect through hardness measurements. Importantly, the key advantage of our method lies in its ability to factorize plastic strain components through elongation measurements, rather than relying solely on work hardening.

Furthermore, this integration of the observational data with the RVE-FE simulations enables the historical average stress triaxiality to be inversely derived using microvoid fraction measurements. Microvoids are primarily formed in DP steel by the fracture of martensite islands, except during microvoid coalescence just before the final fracture [ 49–51 ]. A large proportion of martensite islands, which are compressed by the surrounding ferrite phase, experience a low stress triaxiality [ 52 ]. To account for this, a ductile fracture locus encompassing the low stress triaxiality regime was obtained for single-phase (SP) martensite steel using high-pressure tensile testing at 400 MPa. This locus was subsequently employed to evaluate martensite fracture in RVE-FE simulations under uniaxial tension. The historical average stress triaxiality was then inversely calculated by determining the necessary increase in stress triaxiality from a uniaxial tensile state to match the observed microvoid fraction in the martensite area (volume).

Conventional research on microstructural observations of deformed and fractured regions primarily aimed to elucidate plastic deformation and fracture mechanisms, and to optimize the microstructure based on these findings [ 53–57 ]. While these studies generated valuable knowledge for materials science, the utilization of the knowledge appears to be limited to material development. Their application to engineering processes, such as press-forming process monitoring, is virtually nonexistent. This research is conceived to bridge this gap. Unlike conventional analyses that focused on microscopic perspectives for mechanism elucidation, we introduce, for the first time, the concept of upscaling from microscopic features to macroscopic mechanical quantities. The FE simulation and microstructural analysis presented in this study were developed toward this upscaling approach.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: Two types of DP steels were fabricated in this study and subjected to tensile tests. Subsequently, the morphology of the martensite islands and the microvoid area fraction were evaluated from cross-sectional observations of the tensile fracture regions. These values were then correlated with the macroscopic plastic strain and stress triaxiality in the observation areas using RVE-FE simulations. The detailed procedures are described in the following subsections.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs: Two distinct DP steels with varying martensite volume fractions, designated as DP-A and DP-B, as well as SP ferrite (SP–F) and SP martensite (SP-M) samples, were fabricated in this study under laboratory conditions. The SP steels were designed to emulate the individual phases present in the DP steels and provide the work-hardening curve of each phase for input to the RVE-FE simulations, which is discussed later in this article.

DP steel was selected as it is the most widely used material for automotive applications among various advanced HSSs (AHSSs). Additional reasons for this selection include that, in this material, the martensite islands remain identifiable even after large deformation (whereas ferrite undergoes dislocation-cell formation that makes morphological features unidentifiable) [ 42 ], and that the analysis accuracy remains high even with the homogeneous model assumption in the RVE-FE simulations described later, which make DP steel highly suitable for the post-mortem analysis used in this study.

sections.heading: Material preparation
paragraphs: The DP steels were produced using vacuum-melted cast ingots initially hot-rolled to a thickness of 30 mm. The ingots were heat-treated at 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by a final hot-rolling process at 900 °C to reduce the thickness to 6 mm. The hot-rolled steel sheets were air-cooled to transform austenite to ferrite. To suppress the formation of pearlite, the steel was water-cooled from 650 °C to room temperature, yielding a mixed ferritic and martensitic microstructure. The martensite volume fraction was controlled by adjusting the C concentration in the cast ingots.

SP-F was fabricated using a hot-rolled steel sheet containing 0.01 mass% C, which represents the solid solubility limit; the sheet was initially rough-rolled to a thickness of 30 mm and then heat-treated at 1200 °C for 1 h. The steel sheet was finish-rolled to 6 mm at 900 °C and air-cooled to room temperature, with the ferrite matrix containing 0.01 mass% C. SP-M was fabricated using a cast ingot with 0.4 mass% C (calculated based on the 0.01 mass% C in the ferrite matrix of DP-A) that was rough-rolled at 1200 °C and finish-rolled at 900 °C to a 6 mm thickness, and immediately water-cooled. The martensite was then tempered at 400 °C for 10 min to match the hardness of the martensite in DP steel.

As evident from the heat treatment history described above, martensite islands in DP steel were formed by rapid cooling from the two-phase region at 650 °C, causing austenite transformation. In the as-quenched state, SP-M exhibited significantly higher hardness compared to that of the martensite islands in DP steel, which was attributed to differences in cooling rate and auto-tempering due to the residual heat in DP steel. To achieve a single-phase structure, the rapid cooling from 900 °C was necessary. The hardness difference was adjusted by tempering SP-M. When the hardnesses are identical (i.e., when the maximum tensile strength levels are equivalent), since martensite has a low work-hardening rate, nearly identical flow stress-strain (plastic) relationships can be assumed. Demonstrating that the ductile fracture conditions of martensite islands in DP steel are similar to those of SP-M is difficult. However, as discussed in Section  4.2 , the stress triaxiality in the tensile specimens, inversely calculated through an integrated method combining microvoid volume fraction from martensite fracture with RVE-FE simulations (incorporating SP-M ductile fracture conditions), showed good agreement with macroscopic values, indicating that the conditions were likely consistent.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs:
Fig. 1 
                             shows the images of the DP-A and DP-B microstructures obtained using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi High-Tech SU5000) operated at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. The samples were prepared using a series of grinding and polishing steps. The samples were sequentially ground using 240, 400, 800, and 1500 grit abrasive papers. The samples were then polished using 3 and 1 μm diamond pastes. The samples were further polished for 20 min sequentially using 0.25 and 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspensions.

The SEM images show that the DP microstructures contain hard martensite islands dispersed within a softer ferrite matrix. Quantitative analyses of these images reveal that DP-A and DP-B exhibit martensite area fractions of 0.10 and 0.29, respectively. Hereafter, these values are referred to as “volume fractions” owing to the near equality of area and volume fractions in sufficiently dispersed martensite islands.

Table 2 
                             lists the volume fractions and grain sizes of each phase and the Vickers hardness values for all the studied materials. Notably, the two DP steels exhibited approximately identical characteristics, except for their martensite volume fractions. Furthermore, the ferrite grain size and hardness values of the phases within the DP steels were successfully replicated in the corresponding SP steels, thus validating their use as phase-specific analogs in subsequent analyses.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs:
The tensile strengths of DP-A and DP-B correspond to the DP600 and DP800 steel grades, respectively.  Fig. 2 
                            a shows the nominal stress-strain curve for DP-A and DP-B, obtained using Japanese Industrial Standard (JIS) 14A 3-mm diameter round-bar tensile specimens whose geometry is depicted in  Fig. 2 b. Tensile tests were conducted using an AG-250kN universal testing machine (Shimadzu Corporation). The tensile specimens were machined from the test steels and circumferentially polished using 800- to 1200-grit emery paper. The notched and small round-bar tensile specimens described later in the article were also manufactured using the same procedure.

As shown in  Fig. 2 a, DP-A and DP-B exhibit tensile strengths in the 500 and 700 MPa ranges, respectively.  Fig. 2 a also shows the nominal stress-strain curve for the SP steels. SP-F, which was enhanced by the addition of Si, exhibits a higher tensile strength than ordinary mild steel (270 MPa), with its tensile strength approaching that of DP-A. Previous studies demonstrated that the work-hardening curve of a ferrite matrix is comparable to, albeit slightly lower than, that of DP600 steel [ 60–62 ]. SP-M exhibits a tensile strength of approximately 1.5 GPa and an elongation exceeding 0.1. The elongation value of SP-M indicates that it exhibits ductile fracture behavior, which is characterized by plastic deformation before fracture.

sections.heading: Post-mortem evaluation of martensite island deformation
paragraphs: The elongation of martensite islands was estimated through cross-sectional observations of the tensile fracture regions. The macroscopic strain was evaluated using the observed CSAR. RVE-FE simulations of the DP steels were performed, using the tensile properties of the SP steels as inputs to calibrate the relationship between the martensite island elongation and the macroscopic plastic strain in the observation regions. The stress triaxiality experienced at the observation areas was determined using the RVE-FE simulation results and the actual microvoid area fractions.

sections.heading: RVE models with virtual DP microstructures
paragraphs:
Fig. 8 
                                shows the RVE-FE models. Virtual DP models containing 512 × 256 × 256 voxels were generated and subsequently converted to quadratic tetrahedral elements. The Volume-CAD software package (RIKEN, Japan) was used for the voxel-to-tetra conversion. An elongated RVE shape was selected to closely approximate the dimensions of the small round-bar specimens used in the actual tensile tests. Virtual microstructures were generated using the virtual DP generator previously developed by Matsuno et al. [ 75 ]. This generator randomly assigns 4,000 mother points, divides the three-dimensional cell into Voronoi regions based on these points, and designates each region as either ferrite or martensite. Assigning adjacent regions as martensite resulted in the formation of a single martensite island with a necked shape, similar to the experimentally observed structure of the martensite grains [ 44 , 45 ]. The resulting RVEs yielded martensite volume fractions of approximately 10 % (DP-A,  Fig. 8 a and c) and 29 % (DP-B,  Fig. 8 b and d).

Constraints were applied in these RVE-FE simulations, as illustrated in  Fig. 9 
                               , to maintain all surfaces as planes. The constraint on one side of the surface represents a 1/8 symmetry. Additional constraints were introduced on all surfaces to prevent necking due to deformation inhomogeneity. To numerically achieve a martensite strain equivalent to the  
                                  
                                     
                                        ε 
                                        M 
                                     
                                  
                                observed near the fracture area (as shown in  Fig. 7 a), which is significantly large, a tensile deformation exceeding 70 % was applied. The significantly large strain also necessitated the implementation of the constraints. Notably, although periodic boundary conditions may further improve the simulation results, they require specialized meshes for the boundaries. In this study, simple planar constraints were employed owing to the complexities of mesh generation.

Since the FE simulations cannot account for size effects, the size of the RVEs was maintained based on the number of voxels. In this study, each RVE represents the tensile deformation of the corresponding DP steel, containing approximately 3,200 martensite islands, based on the 1/8 symmetry boundary conditions. Although the 1/8 symmetry model cannot handle infinitely large domain-like periodic conditions, previous studies reported that this number of martensite islands is sufficiently large to represent the macroscopic behavior [ 59 , 76–79 ]. Indeed, the stress-strain curves show good agreement in  Fig. 10 
                               , described later.

sections.heading: Material modeling
paragraphs: The von Mises yield criterion was employed as the material model to simplify each phase, and its respective work-hardening curves were incorporated into the RVE-FE models. Observational studies have demonstrated that homogeneous models adequately capture the strain partitioning within each phase and the martensite fracture behavior [ 52 , 76–80 ]. Since our objective was not to analyze local behavior around individual martensite islands but rather to conduct RVE-FE simulations for estimating the macroscopic stress and strain distribution, we employed a simplified model based on homogeneous assumptions, which included a large number of martensite islands as shown in  Fig. 8 . It should be noted that this simplification is not a compromise but rather an essential requirement to achieve quantitative accuracy in meso-to-macro upscaling. In the subsequent inverse identification, local stress and strain distributions based on inaccurate parameters arising from detailed micromechanisms would become noise, and computational time limitations impose constraints on model size.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: This section presents an analysis of the post-mortem evaluation results from Section  3 , focusing on verification and validation. To validate the accuracy of the stress triaxiality assessments, tensile FE simulations were performed to visualize the actual stress triaxiality in the observation regions. Furthermore, this section explores potential applications of our post-mortem technique.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: An inverse calculation method was developed in this study to determine the quasi-macroscopic tensile strain and the historical average stress triaxiality during tensile deformation, using the deformed microstructure of DP steels. This method leverages the distinctive characteristic that martensite islands remain recognizable even after large deformations, with their aspect ratios increasing proportionally with the tensile deformation. A relationship between the martensite island morphology and the macroscopic tensile strain in the observed region (360 × 240 μm) was established by combining SEM observations with RVE-FE simulations of virtual DP steel models. The historical average stress triaxiality was successfully determined through microvoid area fraction analyses employing the ductile fracture locus of single-phase martensite steel obtained from multiple tensile tests. To align the numerical and observational results, the stress triaxiality increment was inversely calculated by considering the multi-axial state of the observed region.

The proposed microstructure feature-driven derivation method demonstrated excellent agreement with the experimental observations for the two DP steels analyzed. Analyses revealed that the true fracture strain at crack formation, calculated from the macroscopic strain near the fracture area, is smaller than the CSAR-derived values, owing to macroscopic crack formation. The historical average stress triaxialities in the fracture region exhibited values characteristic of multiaxial stress states, with lower values observed in the DP steel containing higher martensite volume fractions. Notably, the post-mortem derivation of the stress triaxiality agreed qualitatively with this trend and quantitatively with the macroscopic FE tensile test simulations, particularly for the DP steel with lower martensite volume fractions.

Future studies will focus on extending this method to determine mechanical quantities from martensite island morphological changes in various deformation modes simulating actual press forming processes.
